1Outcome

Each participant is only subject to a restrictive practice that meets any state and territory authorisation (however described) requirements and the relevant requirements and safeguards outlined in Commonwealth legislation and policy.

2Quality indicators

(1)

Knowledge and understanding of regulated restrictive practices as described in the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018 and knowledge and understanding of any relevant state or territory legislation and/or policy requirements and processes for obtaining authorisation (however described) for the use of any restrictive practices included in a behaviour support plan.

Our commitment: Policy C1, Policy C2. Proof: Register.

(2)

Each Behaviour Support Practitioner undertakes professional development to maintain an understanding of practices considered restrictive and the risks associated with those practices.

Our commitment: Policy C3. Proof: Register.

(3)

Each participant and, with the participant’s consent, their support network, providers implementing behaviour support plans, and other relevant stakeholders are engaged in discussions about the need for restrictive practices and they understand the risks associated with their use. Alternatives to the use of restrictive practices are promoted as part of these discussions.

Our commitment: Policy C4, Policy C5, Policy C6, Policy C14. Proof: Register.

(4)

Each participant and, with the participant’s consent, their support network, their providers implementing behaviour support plans and other relevant stakeholders are engaged in the development of behaviour support strategies that are proportionate to the risk of harm to the participant or others.

Our commitment: Policy C4, Policy C7, Policy C8. Proof: Register.

(5)

Restrictive practices are only included in a participant’s behaviour support plan in accordance with relevant Commonwealth legislation and/or policy requirements and relevant state or territory legislation and/or policy requirements for obtaining authorisation (however described) for the use of any restrictive practices.

Our commitment: Policy C1, Policy C9, Policy C13. Proof: Register.

(6)

Regulated restrictive practices in behaviour support plans comply with the conditions prescribed in the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

Our commitment: Policy C8, Policy C9, Policy C14. Proof: Register.

(7)

Each participant’s behaviour support plan or interim behaviour support plan includes strategies that will lead to the reduction and elimination of any restrictive practices included in the plan.

Our commitment: Policy C7, Policy C10, Policy C12. Proof: Register.

(8)

Support is provided to other providers implementing a behaviour support plan , in delivering services, implementing strategies in the plan and evaluating the effectiveness of current approaches aimed at reducing and eliminating restrictive practices.

Our commitment: Policy C11, Policy C12. Proof: Register.

1Purpose

This policy sets what [Provider name] commits to when a proposes a regulated restrictive practice for a participant's behaviour support . It is for participants, their families and advocates, our practitioners, the providers who carry out our plans, and the people who check our work.

2Applies to

  • Every Behaviour Support Practitioner and at [Provider name], whether an employee or a contractor.
  • Every interim and comprehensive behaviour support plan we write or review that holds, or may come to hold, a regulated restrictive practice.
  • Every state and territory where we work, and every setting where the participant lives or receives supports.
  • Specialist behaviour support only. A provider that only carries out plans, or that also uses a practice itself, follows POL-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Policy for its own use. Its monthly reports follow POL-BSP-05 Monitoring and Reporting the Use of Regulated Restrictive Practices Policy.

"The " in this policy means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. A "practice" is a regulated restrictive practice, one of the five kinds in section 6 of those Rules.

3Commitments

C1

We will write down, for every state and territory where we work, how a restrictive practice is authorised there. Each names the , who must consent, the practices that are prohibited and the evidence to lodge. The Clinical Supervisor checks each note against its source at least every 6 months, and on any announced change to the law, the authorising body's process or its guidance.

Answers: Legislation (1), Legislation (5). How we do it: Procedure step 2, Procedure step 3, Procedure step 30.

C2

We will make sure each Behaviour Support Practitioner knows the Behaviour Support Rules before they propose a practice. They also know the note for each state or territory where they work. They show it again at least every 12 months, in the one annual knowledge check under PRO-SBS-01 step 7, recorded on FRM-HRM-07 Training and Competency Assessment Record and in REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register.

Answers: Legislation (1). How we do it: Procedure step 2, Procedure step 3, Procedure step 30.

C3

We will make sure each Behaviour Support Practitioner does learning on restrictive practices and their risks at least every 12 months. We record it in REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register.

Answers: Legislation (2). How we do it: Procedure step 2, Procedure step 3, Procedure step 30.

C4

We will ask each participant who they want involved before we contact anyone else. We consult and notify the participant, the people they choose, any guardian or other person with legal authority, and each provider that may use the practice. Where the participant refuses to involve a family member or carer, we record the refusal and the reasons as our evidence of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e) of the Behaviour Support Rules, and the Clinical Supervisor records whether any further step is reasonable. We offer an independent advocate and use the communication supports the participant needs.

Answers: Legislation (3), Legislation (4). How we do it: Procedure step 9, Procedure step 10, Procedure step 15, Procedure step 16.

C5

We will give the participant and each person we must notify written notice of our intention to include a practice, in a format they can use. For a comprehensive plan we give it at least 5 before the Clinical Supervisor decides. For an interim plan we give it at the first meeting and at least 2 business days before the decision, so that the consultation fits inside the 1 month limit in section 19(2)(a). Where the risk is immediate, we give it before the plan is finalised and record why.

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 11.

C6

We will explain the risk of harm, the risks of the practice and the alternatives to each person we consult. We ask each person to say the risks back in their own way. We do not treat silence or a signature as understanding. We keep trying with different supports until understanding is shown, or we record what stops it. We record every view and every objection in full.

Answers: Legislation (3). How we do it: Procedure step 12, Procedure step 13, Procedure step 14.

C7

We will build the strategies with the participant, their support network and each . Changes to the environment, new skills and community activities come first. We apply them, or record why we cannot yet, before we rely on a practice.

Answers: Legislation (4), Legislation (7). How we do it: Procedure step 17, Procedure step 20.

C8

We will put a practice in a plan only after the Clinical Supervisor has confirmed in writing that it meets every condition in the Behaviour Support Rules. It must be a , the least restrictive response, in proportion to the risk of harm and used for the shortest possible time. A practitioner never decides on a practice they proposed. The Practitioner lodges every plan that holds a practice with the within 5 business days of finalising it. We do this whether or not is needed or given.

Answers: Legislation (4), Legislation (6). How we do it: Procedure step 18, Procedure step 21, Procedure step 22, Procedure step 23, Procedure step 24.

C9

We will never include a practice that the state or territory prohibits. We will not call a practice authorised until the authorising body has said so in writing. We record its status, conditions and expiry. We tell each implementing provider in writing the same business day if authorisation is declined, lapsed or withdrawn.

Answers: Legislation (5), Legislation (6). How we do it: Procedure step 6, Procedure step 7, Procedure step 25, Procedure step 26.

C10

We will put a in every plan that holds a practice, interim plans included. It sets the steps, the measure, the end point and a review date. For a comprehensive plan the review date is no more than 12 months away. For an interim plan the review date is the comprehensive plan's due date, never 12 months.

Answers: Legislation (7). How we do it: Procedure step 19.

C11

We will support each implementing provider to use a practice only within the plan and its authorisation. Before it first uses the practice, we tell it in writing the conditions of the authorisation and its duties to record and report each use. We agree the data it will collect and the support we will give.

Answers: Legislation (8). How we do it: Procedure step 20, Procedure step 27.

C12

We will check progress towards ending each practice with each implementing provider at least every 3 months. The first check is within 1 month of the plan reaching the provider. We act on what we find.

Answers: Legislation (7), Legislation (8). How we do it: Procedure step 29.

C13

We will act on the same business day we learn that a practice is in use without authorisation, outside the plan or against a prohibition. We tell the implementing provider in writing and open the response under PRO-SBS-05.

Answers: Legislation (5). How we do it: Procedure step 7, Procedure step 8.

C14

We will keep a for every practice and copy its key answers to REG-SBS-01 within 2 business days. We correct a record only with a new entry and a reason. We keep it for 7 years from the day of its last entry.

Answers: Legislation (3), Legislation (6). How we do it: Procedure step 1, Procedure step 28.

C15

We will never include a that the NDIS Commission says must never be in a behaviour support plan, whatever a state or territory authorises. The Commission's guidance on high-risk practices names, among others, prone and supine restraint, pin-downs and take-downs, any restraint that restricts breathing or circulation, punitive or aversive practices, over-correction, and the seclusion of a child. Decision table 2 in PRO-SBS-02 tests this before any other condition, and the Clinical Supervisor keeps the list current against the Commission's guidance.

4Ground rules

G1

A practice is never used as a punishment, for the convenience of workers or because of a shortage of staff. These are never a reason to propose one.

G2

No signature authorises a practice, including the participant's, a guardian's and ours. Only the authorisation process of the state or territory does. Where a state or territory has no process, the conditions of the Behaviour Support Rules still apply.

G3

The practitioner proposes and the Clinical Supervisor decides. Nobody decides on a practice they proposed. A sole practitioner engages an outside Clinical Supervisor in writing before taking any plan that may hold a practice.

G4

A practitioner whose knowledge check or learning is more than 12 months old does not propose or finalise a practice. This holds until the Clinical Supervisor has recorded the learning.

G5

When the law or a state's process is unclear, we treat the practice as needing authorisation. We ask the authorising body or the NDIS Commission before we include it.

G6

For a participant under 18, we consult the person with parental responsibility. We still ask the child for their own view and record it.

G7

The participant decides who is involved from their family, carers and friends. We still consult a person with legal authority over the decision, and the providers who may use the practice, because the law requires it. We tell the participant first and share only what each needs. Where the participant refuses to involve a family member or carer, the refusal and its reasons are our record of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e), and the Clinical Supervisor records whether any further step is reasonable.

G8

We do not shorten a consultation to meet a due date. The 1 month and 6 month plan clocks in the Behaviour Support Rules do not stop. If a date will be missed, we say so, record what is not done and finish it.

G9

A participant, family member, worker or manager who raises a concern about a practice is never punished for it. They can go to the Chief Executive, the independent contact for concerns or the NDIS Commission.

G10

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register shows who holds each one. The Clinical Supervisor is never the practitioner who proposed the practice. A sole practitioner engages an outside Clinical Supervisor in writing. The outside Clinical Supervisor decides on each practice and does the Service Manager's checks on the sole practitioner's own work, including the register-wide checks in How we check that name the Clinical Supervisor; the written agreement says so and what it costs. Everything else the sole practitioner does themselves, including the Quality Manager's role, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the outside Clinical Supervisor with them.

  • The same Rules, sections 8 to 10: prohibited use, authorisation, and use under a plan.

docs.html:
1Purpose

The result: a regulated restrictive practice goes into a participant's behaviour support only after the participant and the people they choose have been consulted. They know the risks and the alternatives. The practice meets the and the process of the state or territory. The plan also holds a way to reduce the practice and end it.

This procedure gives effect to POL-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support), C1 to C15.

"The Behaviour Support Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. A "practice" is a regulated restrictive practice, one of the five kinds in section 6 of those Rules. A "restrictive practice" in the wider sense is any practice or intervention that has the effect of restricting the rights or freedom of movement of a person with disability (NDIS Act 2013, section 9); a practice is regulated only if it meets section 6. A "plan" is an interim or a comprehensive behaviour support plan. A "" is one the 's guidance says must never be in a plan (POL-SBS-02 C15).

2When and who

Start this procedure when any of these happens:

  • A proposes a practice for a new interim or comprehensive plan.
  • A plan review adds, changes or removes a practice.
  • Someone tells you a practice is in use for a participant we write plans for.
  • 3 months have passed since our , our practitioners' learning and our open practice records were last checked (step 30).

Who acts:

  • The Behaviour Support Practitioner leads at steps 1, 2, 4 to 7, 9 to 21, 23 to 27 and 29, and lodges the plan (step 24).
  • The decides whether the practice goes into the plan (step 22). The Clinical Supervisor also keeps the notes and the learning current (steps 3 and 30).
  • The Service Manager opens the response to unauthorised use (step 8), prepares the lodgement and keeps its date and reference (step 24), and copies the record to the REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register practice sheet (step 28).
  • The Chief Executive hears about missed due dates and concerns about managers.
  • The Quality Manager decides whether anything we find is a reportable incident for us, and notifies the NDIS Commission.

Only a provider registered for specialist behaviour support uses this procedure. A provider that only carries out plans uses PRO-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Procedure.

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register shows who holds each role. A sole practitioner is also the Service Manager, the Quality Manager and the Chief Executive, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the outside Clinical Supervisor with them. The Clinical Supervisor is never the practitioner who proposed the practice. A sole practitioner engages an outside Clinical Supervisor in writing before taking any plan that may hold a practice; the outside Clinical Supervisor also does the Service Manager's checks on the sole practitioner's own work.

3Before you start

  • You are a Behaviour Support Practitioner: the Commissioner has considered you suitable to do assessments and write plans that may hold a practice.
  • The plan has a row in REG-SBS-01. The row shows the date we were engaged. It shows when the interim plan is due (1 month after) and when the comprehensive plan is due (6 months after).
  • You have the referral, the assessment so far, and the incident and use records from each .
  • You can open the participant's communication preferences. They are in FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form.
  • You can open the participant's consent record. It is in FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form.
  • You can open REG-QMS-03 Compliance Obligations Register and REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register.
  • You have a blank FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record.

4Watch out

  • A signature is not an authorisation. The participant's, a guardian's and ours do not make a practice lawful. Only the authorisation process of the state or territory does. A practice used without it breaches the registration conditions and can be a reportable incident.
  • Never include a practice the state or territory prohibits. The implementing provider is bound not to use it (Behaviour Support Rules, section 8). A plan that directs it puts the participant at risk and the provider in breach.
  • Never include a high-risk practice the NDIS Commission says must never be in a plan: prone or supine restraint, a pin-down or take-down, a restraint that restricts breathing or circulation, a punitive or aversive practice, over-correction or the seclusion of a child. State or territory authorisation never makes one acceptable. Decision table 2 row 16 tests this first.
  • Silence is not agreement, and being told is not understanding. A person who nods may not have understood. A plan built on that is built on a view the participant does not hold.
  • The plan clocks run while you consult. The interim plan is due 1 month after we are engaged. The comprehensive plan is due 6 months after (Behaviour Support Rules, section 19). Shortening the consultation to meet a date harms the participant and breaks the Rules.
  • Only a prescriber decides what a medicine is for, and what dose. You never decide or change a dose. The plan's chemical restraint protocol copies the medication, dose, route and frequency exactly from the prescriber's current order and names the prescriber and the date of the order; this holds no dose. A wrong decision about a medicine can seriously harm the participant.
  • A single emergency use needs no authorisation first, but it is still a reportable incident. If more use is likely, the participant needs an interim plan (Behaviour Support Rules, sections 9 and 19; Incident Rules, section 16). Handle it at step 7.
  • A practice is never a punishment, a convenience or an answer to short staffing. Any of these is a reason to refuse the proposal.
  • Telling someone the participant has refused can break their trust and their privacy. Contact only the people they chose, plus the person with legal authority and the providers who may use the practice, whom the law requires us to consult. Record each refusal and its reasons: that record is our evidence of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e).
  • If anyone is in immediate danger, call 000 first. Then follow PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure.

Decision table 1: The five kinds of regulated restrictive practice

This table follows section 6 of the Behaviour Support Rules. The primary purpose decides the kind. If you are unsure, treat the practice as regulated and ask the Clinical Supervisor.

If the practice isIt isEveryday examplesIt is not this kind when
The sole confinement of a person in a room or space where they cannot leave, or are made to feel they may notSeclusionA bedroom door locked or held shut from outside. Telling a person to stay in a room and not come outThe person chooses to be alone and can leave whenever they want
A medicine or chemical used for the primary purpose of influencing behaviourChemical restraintA sedating medicine given when a person is agitated, so that they settleA medical practitioner prescribed it to treat, or enable treatment of, a diagnosed mental disorder, physical illness or physical condition
A device used to prevent, restrict or subdue movement, for the primary purpose of influencing behaviourMechanical restraintBed rails raised so a person cannot leave the bed. Straps that hold a person in a chair so they cannot get upThe device has a therapeutic or non-behavioural purpose. Where a health practitioner advised it, ask them to confirm that in writing (our standard)
Physical force used to prevent, restrict or subdue movement of the body or part of it, for the primary purpose of influencing behaviourPhysical restraintHolding a person's arms down. Pinning a person to the floor or a wallA reflexive hands-on technique to guide or redirect a person away from harm, as an act of care. If it is planned, or used to stop a behaviour, ask the Clinical Supervisor
A limit on a person's free access to any part of their environment, including items or activitiesEnvironmental restraintA locked cupboard, fridge or pantry. A door or gate the person cannot open. A phone or a loved item kept out of reach until behaviour changesThe limit does not restrict this person's free access. If you are unsure, the Clinical Supervisor decides and records why
None of the five kinds aboveNot regulated by the Behaviour Support RulesA limit that fits none of the descriptionsThe Clinical Supervisor decides whether it is a regulated restrictive practice under section 6 and, if not, whether the state or territory regulates it. When in doubt we treat it as regulated

7If it goes wrong

IfThen
The participant refuses to talk, leaves, or is too unwell or distressedStop. Do not go on because time is short. Ask what they want. Offer another day, place, format or support person, and an independent advocate. Record what happened at Q18. Never treat silence as agreement. Tell the Service Manager if a due date is at risk
The participant says no to involving a person, now or laterDo not contact that person. Explain that the person with legal authority and each implementing provider must still be consulted, and why. Record the refusal and the participant's reasons at Q9: that is our record of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e), and the Clinical Supervisor records whether any further step is reasonable. If the participant does not want a provider involved, tell them the plan cannot be carried out safely without it. They may choose another provider
The participant or the person with authority objects to the practiceWrite the objection in full at Q16. Do not treat any signature as agreement. Send the objection to the Clinical Supervisor and, at step 25, to the authorising body. The Clinical Supervisor may decide not to include the practice
A person has not understood the risks after you tried twice with different supportsWrite "not yet understood" at Q14 and what you tried. Ask an advocate or a communication specialist to help. Tell the Clinical Supervisor, who decides whether the proposal goes on and records why. The duty to keep trying does not end
People disagree about the practiceWrite each view at Q16 and Q17, the participant's first. Do not choose by the number of people. Follow the authorisation process of the state or territory. The person with legal authority decides what the law gives them to decide
A new provider will carry out the planConsult it at step 16 and agree data and support at step 20. Tell it in writing under step 27 before it first uses the practice. Start a plan review under PRO-SBS-04
The participant moves to another state or territoryAn authorisation is given under one state or territory's process. Read the note for the new one at step 2. Treat the practice as unauthorised there until it is authorised: this is our reading of sections 9(1) and 21(3)(b), and the note records any interstate recognition arrangement. Go to step 7 if it is in use
An implementing provider does not answer within 5 business daysTry a second contact. Tell the Service Manager. If effective engagement with the provider is not possible, or the plan is not being followed, PRO-SBS-04 sets the notice to the Commissioner
A due date will be missed: an interim plan, a comprehensive plan, the notice or the lodgementTell the Service Manager at once. The Service Manager tells the Chief Executive the same business day. Do not shorten the consultation or backdate a record. Write which part is not done and why. Finish it as soon as you can. Record the delay in REG-QMS-01
The practitioner is absent or leavesThe Service Manager gives the record to another practitioner whose learning is current, within 2 business days (our standard). They carry on from the last completed step. The record shows both names
The Clinical Supervisor is absent for more than 3 business daysThe Chief Executive names a backup Clinical Supervisor, never the practitioner who proposed the practice. A sole practitioner has a backup outside Clinical Supervisor named in writing in advance. No practice is included without a decision at step 22
The authorising body declines, is slow, or its process is unclearAsk in writing. Record each reply at Q33. The practice is not used under this plan until it is authorised. If it is already in use, step 7 applies and the interim plan route under PRO-SBS-06 starts
The participant's plan or its authorisation is out of dateTreat the practice as unauthorised from the day the authorisation lapsed. Go to step 7. Start a plan review under PRO-SBS-04 and a new request at step 25
You are pressed to include a practice for convenience, cost or short staffing, or to skip a step or backdate a recordTell the Chief Executive. If the concern is about the Chief Executive, tell the chair of the governing body. In a provider with one owner, tell the independent contact for concerns. You can always phone the NDIS Commission on 1800 035 544. Nobody may punish you for raising it. If you suspect abuse or neglect, follow PRO-SGD-01 Violence, Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation and Discrimination Procedure
A family member or carer is the source of the risk, or you suspect they are harming the participantDo not share the notice with them without the Clinical Supervisor's advice. Follow PRO-SGD-01. The participant's safety and wishes come first
The participant, a family member or an advocate complains about this processFollow PRO-FBK-01 Feedback and Complaints Management Procedure. Tell the Clinical Supervisor. The complaint is recorded in REG-FBK-01 Complaints Register
An entry is wrong or must changeAdd a new entry with the date and the reason. Never overwrite or delete an earlier entry
Someone is hurt or in immediate dangerCall 000. Then follow PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure

8Done means

  • The consultation record is complete, signed by the practitioner and the Clinical Supervisor, and filed on the participant's file in the restricted folder.
  • Each person consulted was given written notice in their format at least 5 business days before the decision (2 business days for an interim plan), or the interim reason is written down.
  • Each person has told us what they understood and what they think, and every objection is recorded in full.
  • The Clinical Supervisor's test at Q28 and decision at Q29 are written, with reasons.
  • The plan holds a reduction and elimination strategy, a review date within 12 months (the comprehensive plan's due date for an interim plan) and an agreed data plan.
  • The plan has been lodged with the Commissioner, with the date and reference recorded.
  • The authorisation status is recorded, and each implementing provider has the conditions and its duties in writing.
  • The REG-SBS-01 practice sheet shows the practice and can be traced to this record.
  • The first progress check is booked.

9Quick card

153 words
  • Tell the implementing provider in writing the same business day if the practice is in use without authorisation, outside the plan or prohibited (step 7)
  • Include no practice that the state or territory prohibits, and no high-risk practice, whatever is authorised (step 6)
  • Give written notice to each person at least 5 business days before the Clinical Supervisor decides, 2 for an interim plan (step 11)
  • Ask each person to say the risks back in their own way (step 13)
  • Write the reduction and elimination strategy before you send the record (step 19)
  • Put no practice in a plan until the Clinical Supervisor has decided (step 22)
  • The Practitioner lodges the plan within 5 business days of finalising it, authorised or not (step 24)
  • Call a practice authorised only when the authorising body has said so in writing (step 26)
  • Check progress with each implementing provider at least every 3 months (step 29)

form.intro:
Use this record whenever a regulated restrictive practice is proposed for a participant's behaviour support plan, or is already in one. It shows who we talked with and which risks we explained. It shows which alternatives came first and why the practice is in proportion to the risk. It also shows how the practice will be reduced and ended.

This record authorises no restrictive practice. Only the authorisation process of the state or territory can do that.

Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses this record. A provider that only carries out plans uses FRM-BSP-03 Restrictive Practice Authorisation and Consent Record.

  • One record covers one participant and one plan. Start a new record for each new plan, and for each review that adds, changes or removes a practice.
  • Answer questions 4 to 7, 12 to 17 and 19 to 35 once for each practice. The register keeps one row per practice per plan (the REG-SBS-01 practice sheet), so these answers are copied per practice.
  • The completes the record as each step of PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) is done. The record is in the order of the steps.
  • The Clinical Supervisor answers questions 28 and 29.
  • The practitioner adds a dated entry at question 35 after every progress check. Never overwrite an earlier entry.

Have ready:

  • The referral and the assessment so far.
  • The participant's communication preferences, in FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form.
  • The participant's consent record, in FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form.
  • The incident and use records from each implementing provider.
  • The state or territory note, in REG-QMS-03 Compliance Obligations Register.
  • The practitioner's row in REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register.

What happens next: the Service Manager copies each answer marked REG-SBS-01 to the row for this practice and this plan on the practice sheet of REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register, in the column the question protocol pins. The record stays on the participant's file with the plan.
form.privacy:
We collect this information to decide whether a restrictive practice can be justified. We also use it to seek authorisation and to plan how to end the practice. The Behaviour Support Rules require us to consult the participant and the people around them. They also require us to lodge the plan with the .

The practitioner, the Clinical Supervisor and the Service Manager read this record. We give parts of it to the of the state or territory and to the NDIS Commission. We share it with a provider that carries out the plan only as the law requires or the participant agrees. The same goes for the participant's support network. The law requires us to consult the providers who may use the practice and any person with legal authority, even if you ask us not to; we will tell you first and share only what they need.

If you are the participant, you can see this record and ask us to correct it. You can have an advocate with you. You can tell us you disagree, and we will write that down in your words.

POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store and protect this record.
form.after:
• Practitioner: send the record to the Clinical Supervisor with the draft plan, before the plan is finalised.
  • Clinical Supervisor: answer questions 28 and 29 within 5 business days of receiving the record and the draft plan, or 2 business days for an interim plan (our standard).
  • Service Manager: copy each answer marked REG-SBS-01 to the practice sheet row within 2 business days of each entry (our standard).
  • Practitioner: update question 33 on the day the authorisation status changes.
  • Practitioner: lodge the plan and answer question 31 within 5 business days of the plan being finalised (our standard). The Service Manager prepares the lodgement and keeps the date and reference.
  • Practitioner: add an entry at question 35 after each progress check. Checks are at least every 3 months while the practice is in the plan.
  • File the record on the participant's file with the plan, in a restricted folder.
  • Keep it for 7 years from the day of the last entry (our standard). The law of [state or territory] can require longer.

register.proves:
This register is the one running record of every behaviour support [Provider name] writes. It has three sheets. On the plan sheet each row is one plan version. It shows when we were engaged and who wrote the plan. It shows what the participant agreed to and which accepted the plan. It shows whether the plan reached the Commissioner on time and when it is next due for review. On the practice sheet each row is one regulated restrictive practice in one plan, keyed on the plan number in col A, and holds the answers FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record routes here, with every status the practice has held. On the incident review sheet each row is one review under FRM-SBS-06 Restrictive Practice Incident Review Record of an emergency or unauthorised use, keyed on the plan number in col A.

"" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

  • Indicators evidenced: s 40 (1) to s 40 (6). The register also holds the plan dates and records that s 39, s 41, s 42, s 43 and s 44 rely on. Those threads write to the columns marked with their indicators.
  • Legal basis: the Behaviour Support Rules. Sections 17 and 18 say who writes. Section 19 sets time limits. Section 20 says how plans are developed and section 21 what they contain. Sections 22 to 24 cover review, form and lodgement.
  • Retention: keep each row for 7 years from the day the plan is superseded or ends (our standard). We set it to match the 7 years in section 15(3) of the Behaviour Support Rules for records of the use of a regulated restrictive practice.
  • Other law can require longer, for example for records about a child. For a participant under 18, keep the row until they turn 25 or for 7 years, whichever is later (our standard pending state law). Check REG-INF-02 Records Retention and Disposal Register and the law of [state or territory] before any row is destroyed.

Columns H and I are worked out and never typed over. Columns AB, AC, AD and AW are filled only when col Z lists a regulated restrictive practice, and summarise the practice sheet. Columns AN to AP are filled only when col AM is yes. Columns AR to BA are filled from the forms named in the Filled from column. The practice sheet columns RP-A to RP-R are filled from FRM-SBS-02, one row per practice per plan. The incident review sheet columns IR-A to IR-O are filled from FRM-SBS-06, one row per review; col AZ summarises them.
register.entry:
1. The Service Manager opens the row and keeps it. A sole Practitioner does both. Open the row on the day we confirm the referral (our standard).
  2. Use one row for each plan version. A new version is a new row. Link it to the one it replaces in col D and col BD.
  3. The Practitioner gives each answer to the Service Manager within 1 of recording it on the form. The forms are FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template and FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record for the plan sheet, and FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record for the practice sheet. The Service Manager enters it within 2 business days of the stage (our standard).
  4. Columns that hold a list (col R, col Z, col AC, col AD, col AG, col AK, col AW and col BB, and practice sheet cols RP-P and RP-R) take a new dated line for each change. Never overwrite a line. An authorisation status is never typed over: every status the practice has held stays visible with its date.
  5. Never overwrite or delete an entry. A correction is a new version of the row, with the date, your name and the reason.
  6. Never type over a worked-out date. To change the engagement date in col F, record the reason and the name of the who agreed.
  7. When systems are down, use the paper forms. The Service Manager enters them within 2 business days of the system coming back.
  8. When a row is about the work of the Service Manager or the Practitioner who keeps it, the Chief Executive holds it. When it is about the Chief Executive, the holds it. In a sole practitioner provider the Practitioner keeps every row, and the outside Clinical Supervisor reviews them every month under How we review.
  9. The practice sheet is the second sheet of this register: one row per regulated restrictive practice per plan, keyed on the plan number in col A, with cols RP-A to RP-R. Open a practice row when col Z first lists or proposes the practice. The incident review sheet is the third sheet: one row per FRM-SBS-06 review, keyed on col A, with cols IR-A to IR-O; open a row when a review starts and summarise it in col AZ. A small provider can keep the other list columns on a further sheet in the same way; each line carries the plan number from col A.

A row is closed only when all of these are true:

  • the plan has been replaced by a later version that is in force, or the plan has ended, or the participant has left us, and col BD says which
  • every lodgement is done and recorded in col AO
  • every open line in col BB is done, or has moved to REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register with an owner and a due date
  • the Service Manager has checked the row and recorded the closing date.

register.rows: The rows are the data. They are kept in the workbook or system built to this specification, not in this document. The register has three sheets: the plan sheet (one row per plan version, cols A to BF), the practice sheet (one row per regulated restrictive practice per plan, cols RP-A to RP-R, keyed on col A) and the incident review sheet (one row per FRM-SBS-06 review, cols IR-A to IR-O, keyed on col A). Where a plan sheet cell would otherwise hold a list of practices or reviews, the second or third sheet holds the detail and the plan sheet cell summarises it.
